verdicts.reason: Identifies the challenged tax as the section 965 Mandatory Repatriation Tax and cites §§ 965(a), (c), (d).
Explains the MRT as a one-time, backward-looking attribution of accumulated undistributed foreign-corporation income to U.S. shareholders.
Identifies KisanKraft as the Indian American-controlled foreign corporation that generated substantial income.
States that KisanKraft had not distributed the income to its American shareholders as of 2017.
Reports the Moores’ 13-percent ownership interest rather than treating them as sole owners.
Reports approximately $508,000 pre-deduction pro rata accumulated income and separately $132,512 in declared MRT income.
Reports $14,729 owed and paid, followed by the refund suit.
Mentions § 951A only as a possible statutory issue and does not treat Moore as deciding GILTI constitutionality.
Frames the dispute as direct-tax/property characterization versus an income tax and notes the Court rejected the unapportioned direct-tax-on-property theory.
Distinguishes income realized by KisanKraft from receipt by the shareholder and says the MRT taxes the shareholders’ attributed share of entity income.
Explains that, in the decided circumstances, Congress may attribute realized entity income to shareholders and tax them on it.
Uses partnership taxation as an attribution analogue in describing the Court’s precedents without asserting all entities are legally identical.
Mentions S corporations as part of the precedent line but does not address the consent rationale or explain why shareholder consent alone does not establish constitutional authority.
Compares the MRT to subpart F and describes foreign-corporation attribution as part of longstanding congressional practice.
Explains that Macomber involved a stock dividend and was not an attribution holding prohibiting entity-income attribution.
States the Moores’ constructive-realization distinction and the majority’s rejection of it by comparing the MRT to subpart F and pass-through taxes.
Lists shareholder taxation as the first express boundary of the narrow holding.
Retains the requirement that the attributed income be undistributed income realized by the entity.
Retains the requirement that the income be attributed to the shareholders.
Retains the condition that the entity itself has not been taxed on that income.
States expressly that the Court did not decide whether realization is constitutionally required.
Does not present a wealth or net-worth tax as upheld; it notes such taxes were left for another day.
Does not treat an unapportioned appreciation tax as resolved and notes the Court left that issue open.
Identifies the Due Process Clause constraint on arbitrary attribution.
Discusses the reserved same-undistributed-income double-taxation scenario but does not distinguish it from ordinary corporate-level tax followed by shareholder dividend tax.
States that the Ninth Circuit was affirmed and that the MRT challenge failed.
Labels Justice Jackson’s broad tax-power and anti-realization-requirement views as a concurrence while separately describing the majority’s narrow holding.
Describes Justice Barrett’s concurrence in the judgment as disagreeing with the majority’s reasoning and reserving different-tax issues.
Identifies Justice Thomas’s realization/attribution position as a dissent, not the controlling opinion.
Treats the petitioner brief’s realization arguments as advocacy and contrasts them with the final majority holding.
Requests facts on ownership, entity realization, attribution relationship, and prior entity-level tax before evaluating another tax theory.
Separates the likely foreclosed no-distribution MRT theory from reserved due-process, double-taxation, and statutory/procedural claims.
